title: Ang 318–323: Gauri ki Var M5
tomorrow: did Simran pass? and what did a weaver ask about birth?

lines: HOW WAS YOUR DAY? A SCORE.
cards: How was your day? Usually the answer is a score: good if it went your way, bad if it didn't.

Today is Simran's driving test, 10:40, her dad in the waiting room, Maya texting from school, Bebe's Sukhmani path done before breakfast. Pass, and it's a great day. Fail, and it's the worst one of the year.
That's the math, anyway. Guru Arjan's ballad in Gauri, from Ang 318, works it out differently.

teach.b: The question is old: what makes a day good?

teach.h: THE DAY GOD COMES TO MIND.
teach.b: Guru Arjan's ballad sets short saloks of his own between its stanzas, and one of them answers, in paraphrase: Nanak, beautiful is the day when God comes to mind; cursed is even a fine season when the Supreme Lord is forgotten.
So a day's worth has nothing to do with the result. A day is beautiful when the Lord comes to mind. A perfect spring is a loss if you spent it forgetting.

Here's the unity thread. The Psalms, sung by Jews and Christians, have a line that leans the same way. In the King James Version: "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it."
Shared ground: the goodness of a day comes from God, not from the scoreboard. Two old songs, from two families of faith, turned toward the same sky. And one honest difference.

teach.h: PSALM 118: THE DAY THE LORD MADE.
teach.b: The psalm calls the day good because the Lord made it, and calls for joy in it. The salok puts the weight on the person: the same day is beautiful or wasted depending on whether God comes to mind.
One looks to the day's maker; the other to the heart that remembers.

how: Guru Arjan's Gauri ki Var is read in the Granth's order and sung as kirtan; Sikhs keep the Name in mind through the day as simran, and Jews and Christians sing Psalm 118 in worship.

games.q: your aunt says her beach vacation felt hollow, but a hard week at the hospital with her mom felt close to God. what would the salok say?
o: the hard week was the beautiful one: God came to mind in it.
the vacation was the good week; feelings don't change the facts.
both weeks were bad, since one was hollow and one was hard.
games.why: in Guru Arjan's salok a day is beautiful when God comes to mind, and even a fine season is lost in forgetting. the result doesn't decide it.

practice: Count back through today, or yesterday if today has barely started, and stop at each moment something good came to mind: a face, a meal, a kindness, a breath that came easy. Don't score them.
Just count them, one finger at a time, and rest on the last one.
